\section{Introduction}
Spectral graph theory translates combinatorial structure into matrix eigenvalues. A spectral statistic is particularly revealing when it also has a transparent local meaning. The Seidel matrix, a signed encoding of a graph, provides such an example.

Its first moment vanishes, while its second moment is $n(n-1)$ for every graph of order $n$. These moments therefore contain no edge-sensitive information beyond graph order. The cubic moment is the first place where products around nontrivial closed walks appear. We show that
\[
\tr(S^3)=\sum_{i,j,k}w(i,j,k)=6(N_{\mathrm{even}}-N_{\mathrm{odd}}),
\]
where $w$ is the parity sign of an ordered triple, and $N_{\mathrm{even}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{odd}}$ count three-vertex subsets inducing an even and odd number of edges.

The sign product is also a discrete holonomy. Under switching, $S_{ij}$ becomes $d_iS_{ij}d_j$ with $d_i^2=1$. Every vertex factor occurs twice around a triangle and cancels. This local argument explains invariance of the cubic moment and extends naturally to closed walks of every length.

\section{Definitions and elementary moments}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph and let $n=|V|$.

\begin{definition}[Seidel matrix]
The Seidel matrix $S$ of $G$ is the real $V\times V$ matrix
\[
S_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0,&i=j,\\
-1,&i\ne j\text{ and }\{i,j\}\in E,\\
+1,&i\ne j\text{ and }\{i,j\}\notin E.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

The matrix is real symmetric and has real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$.

\begin{definition}[Moments and energy]
For $m\geq1$, the $m$th Seidel moment and the Seidel energy are
\[
M_m(G)=\tr(S^m)=\sum_{r=1}^n\lambda_r^m,
\qquad
\ES(G)=\sum_{r=1}^n|\lambda_r|.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[First moment]
Every finite simple graph satisfies $\tr(S)=0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every diagonal entry is zero, and the trace is their sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Graph-independent second moment]
Every simple graph on $n$ vertices satisfies
\[
\tr(S^2)=n(n-1).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Symmetry gives $(S^2)_{ii}=\sum_jS_{ij}^2=n-1$: the diagonal term is zero and every other term is one. Summing over $i$ proves the claim.
\end{proof}

Thus $\sum_r\lambda_r=0$ and $\sum_r\lambda_r^2=n(n-1)$. In particular,
\[
\ES(G)=\|\lambda\|_1\geq\|\lambda\|_2=\sqrt{n(n-1)}.
\]
Equality in the norm inequality occurs only when at most one coordinate is nonzero; for $n>1$, trace zero rules this out for a Seidel matrix. The bound is therefore a scale constraint rather than a sharp equality classification.

\section{Triple parity and the cubic moment}
\begin{definition}[Parity weight]
For $(i,j,k)\in V^3$, define
\[
w_G(i,j,k)=\begin{cases}
0,&i=j\text{ or }j=k\text{ or }k=i,\\
-1,&i,j,k\text{ distinct and spanning an odd number of edges},\\
+1,&i,j,k\text{ distinct and spanning an even number of edges}.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Local product--parity identity]
For every ordered triple,
\[
S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}=w_G(i,j,k).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a vertex repeats, one factor is diagonal and therefore zero. Otherwise every edge contributes $-1$ and every nonedge contributes $+1$, so the product is $(-1)^e$, where $e$ is the number of induced edges.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Signed-Triangle Moment Theorem]
For every finite simple graph,
\[
\tr(S^3)=\sum_{i\in V}\sum_{j\in V}\sum_{k\in V}w_G(i,j,k).
\]
Thus the cubic moment is the number of even-edge ordered triples of distinct vertices minus the number of odd-edge ordered triples.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Matrix multiplication yields
\[
\tr(S^3)=\sum_i(S^3)_{ii}=\sum_{i,j,k}S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}.
\]
Apply the local product--parity identity term by term.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Unordered triple formula]
Let $N_{\mathrm{even}}$ count three-element vertex sets inducing zero or two edges, and let $N_{\mathrm{odd}}$ count those inducing one or three edges. Then
\[
\tr(S^3)=6(N_{\mathrm{even}}-N_{\mathrm{odd}}).
\]
Consequently, $\tr(S^3)=0$ exactly when the two parity classes have equal size.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Each three-element set has six orderings, all with the same parity sign. Triples with repeated vertices contribute zero.
\end{proof}

For the empty graph on three vertices the cubic trace is $6$; for the complete graph it is $-6$. Both have second moment $6$, showing exactly what the cubic statistic adds.

\section{Switching as local gauge symmetry}
Choose signs $d_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ and put $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)$. The switched matrix is $S'=DSD$, with $S'_{ij}=d_iS_{ij}d_j$. Graphically, this toggles adjacency across the cut between vertices carrying opposite selected signs.

\begin{theorem}[Triangle-Holonomy Invariance]
For every ordered triple $(i,j,k)$,
\[
S'_{ij}S'_{jk}S'_{ki}=S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expanding the left side gives
\[
(d_iS_{ij}d_j)(d_jS_{jk}d_k)(d_kS_{ki}d_i).
\]
The vertex factors combine to $d_i^2d_j^2d_k^2=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cubic switching invariance]
Diagonal sign switching preserves the cubic moment:
\[
\tr((S')^3)=\tr(S^3).
\]
It also preserves $N_{\mathrm{even}}-N_{\mathrm{odd}}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Sum the invariant triangular products and invoke the unordered triple formula.
\end{proof}

The product around a triangle is a holonomy: edge signs depend on vertex gauge choices, while the product around a closed route does not. More generally, for a closed walk $v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m=v_0$, the product $\prod_{t=0}^{m-1}S_{v_tv_{t+1}}$ is switching invariant because all vertex signs cancel. Summing over closed walks gives a combinatorial explanation of switching invariance for every moment $\tr(S^m)$.

Suppose $\{a,b\}$ is an edge and let $G^-=G-\{a,b\}$. Its deletion changes $S_{ab}=S_{ba}=-1$ to $+1$, so

Only three-vertex subsets containing both $a$ and $b$ change parity.

Deleting $\{a,b\}$ changes the cubic moment by
\[
\tr((S^-)^3)-\tr(S^3)=12(S^2)_{ab}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For every $c\notin\{a,b\}$, the triple $\{a,b,c\}$ has six orderings. Flipping the sign of $S_{ab}$ reverses each ordering's product. If the original cyclic product is $q=S_{ab}S_{bc}S_{ca}$, that unordered triple contributes $-12q$ to the change. Since $S_{ab}=-1$, summing gives
\[
12\sum_cS_{ac}S_{cb}=12(S^2)_{ab};
\]
the diagonal terms vanish.
\end{proof}

This identity equates a rank-two matrix perturbation with a local parity census. The entry $(S^2)_{ab}$ is the signed imbalance among possible third vertices.

\section{Algorithms}
A direct dense method constructs $S$ in $O(n^2)$ time and computes $S^2$, $S^3$, or the eigenvalues in $O(n^3)$ time. It simultaneously supplies spectral moments and energy.

An exact combinatorial method iterates through the $\binom n3$ unordered vertex triples. It counts the three induced edges, adds $+1$ for even parity and $-1$ for odd parity, and multiplies the balance by six. This uses $O(n^3)$ time and constant auxiliary space beyond the graph representation.

Switching by a sign vector costs $O(n^2)$ entry operations. For a single edge deletion, if $S^2$ is already known, the cubic update is read in constant time; computing only $(S^2)_{ab}$ directly costs $O(n)$. Thus a global trace admits a local incremental update.

\section{Applications and limitations}
The cubic trace is a signed induced-subgraph statistic. It compresses the four possible edge counts on three vertices into an even--odd balance. This is exactly the information compatible with multiplication of Seidel signs.

Triangle products are invariants of switching classes and form the elementary data underlying two-graphs. Since $D^2=I$, switching also makes $DSD$ similar to $S$ and therefore preserves the whole spectrum. Consequently every spectral quantity, including Seidel energy, is constant within a switching class; it cannot be a strict monotone there.

Edge deletion is different. It is a rank-two update, not generally a switching. The first two moments remain fixed, while the cubic moment responds through $(S^2)_{ab}$. This matters for the conjecture that deleting any edge of a Tur\'an graph $T(n,r)$ strictly increases Seidel energy when $r\geq4$ and $n\geq4r$. The universal second moment cannot decide the question. The cubic update supplies a first diagnostic, but energy depends on all absolute eigenvalues and especially on motion across zero, so quotient spectra and finer perturbation formulas are needed.

The cubic moment does not recover the full distribution of three-vertex induced subgraphs. Nor do a few moments determine the spectrum in general. Higher moments add signed closed-walk data; sufficiently many power sums recover the characteristic polynomial through Newton identities.

\section{Future directions}
The unordered formula should first be applied systematically to structured graph families. For edge deletion, classifying third vertices by their adjacency to the deleted endpoints gives a direct count of $(S^2)_{ab}$.

A general closed-walk holonomy theorem would provide a unified combinatorial proof of switching invariance of $\tr(S^m)$ for every $m$. Combined with Newton identities, this leads from local gauge cancellation to characteristic-polynomial invariance.

For the rank-two update
\[
S'=S+2(e_ae_b^{\mathsf T}+e_be_a^{\mathsf T}),
\]
the matrix determinant lemma reduces $\det(xI-S')$ to a $2\times2$ determinant involving entries of $(xI-S)^{-1}$. Interlacing and zero-crossing analysis may then control changes in Seidel energy, particularly for Tur\'an graphs whose symmetry supports quotient reduction.

Extremal energy questions require care. A fixed second moment alone gives $\|\lambda\|_1\geq\|\lambda\|_2$, whose equality case has at most one nonzero coordinate. Equal-magnitude conference spectra do not attain equality in this elementary bound. Any sharper classification must incorporate trace zero, realizability, multiplicities, and graph structure.

\section{Conclusion}
The cubic Seidel moment is an exact signed census of triangle parity:
\[
\tr(S^3)=6(N_{\mathrm{even}}-N_{\mathrm{odd}}).
\]
Switching factors cancel locally around every triangle, preserving each holonomy and the total trace. Deleting one edge reverses precisely the triangles through that edge and yields
\[
\Delta\tr(S^3)=12(S^2)_{ab}.
\]
These formulas connect spectral moments, induced-subgraph enumeration, and discrete gauge symmetry. They identify the cubic moment as the first edge-sensitive statistic beyond the universal Seidel sphere and provide a natural foundation for higher-moment and edge-perturbation analysis.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Iterable, Sequence

Matrix = list[list[int]]
Edge = tuple[int, int]


def normalize_edges(edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> set[Edge]:
    """Return undirected edges as sorted endpoint pairs."""
    return {tuple(sorted((a, b))) for a, b in edges if a != b}


def seidel_matrix(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Matrix:
    """Construct the n-by-n Seidel matrix of a finite simple graph."""
    edge_set = normalize_edges(edges)
    return [
        [0 if i == j else (-1 if tuple(sorted((i, j))) in edge_set else 1)
         for j in range(n)]
        for i in range(n)
    ]


def matmul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Multiply two square integer matrices."""
    n = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(n))
             for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def trace(a: Matrix) -> int:
    """Return the trace of a square matrix."""
    return sum(a[i][i] for i in range(len(a)))


def spectral_moments(s: Matrix) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Return the first three exact moments tr(S), tr(S^2), tr(S^3)."""
    s2 = matmul(s, s)
    s3 = matmul(s2, s)
    return trace(s), trace(s2), trace(s3)


def triangle_parity_counts(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Count unordered vertex triples with even and odd induced edge counts."""
    edge_set = normalize_edges(edges)
    even = odd = 0
    for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
        count = sum(
            tuple(sorted(pair)) in edge_set
            for pair in ((i, j), (j, k), (k, i))
        )
        if count % 2 == 0:
            even += 1
        else:
            odd += 1
    return even, odd


def switch_matrix(s: Matrix, signs: Sequence[int]) -> Matrix:
    """Apply diagonal sign switching S_ij -> d_i S_ij d_j."""
    if len(s) != len(signs) or any(d not in (-1, 1) for d in signs):
        raise ValueError("signs must contain one value in {-1,+1} per vertex")
    return [[signs[i] * s[i][j] * signs[j] for j in range(len(s))]
            for i in range(len(s))]


def delete_edge(edges: Iterable[Edge], edge: Edge) -> set[Edge]:
    """Delete one undirected edge from an edge set."""
    result = normalize_edges(edges)
    target = tuple(sorted(edge))
    if target not in result:
        raise ValueError(f"{target} is not an edge")
    result.remove(target)
    return result


def demonstrate_triangle_identity() -> None:
    """Compare cubic matrix traces with six times the parity imbalance."""
    examples = {
        "empty triangle": (3, set()),
        "complete triangle": (3, {(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)}),
        "five-cycle": (5, {(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0)}),
    }
    print("1. Cubic trace as signed triple parity")
    for name, (n, edges) in examples.items():
        moments = spectral_moments(seidel_matrix(n, edges))
        even, odd = triangle_parity_counts(n, edges)
        parity_value = 6 * (even - odd)
        assert moments[2] == parity_value
        assert moments[0] == 0 and moments[1] == n * (n - 1)
        print(f"   {name:18s}: moments={moments}, "
              f"(N_even,N_odd)=({even},{odd}), 6Δ={parity_value}")


def demonstrate_switching() -> None:
    """Show that triangle holonomy and the cubic trace survive switching."""
    n = 6
    edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 5)}
    signs = (-1, 1, -1, 1, 1, -1)
    s = seidel_matrix(n, edges)
    switched = switch_matrix(s, signs)
    before = spectral_moments(s)
    after = spectral_moments(switched)
    for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
        lhs = switched[i][j] * switched[j][k] * switched[k][i]
        rhs = s[i][j] * s[j][k] * s[k][i]
        assert lhs == rhs
    assert before == after
    print("\n2. Switching invariance")
    print(f"   signs={signs}")
    print(f"   moments before={before}, after={after}")
    print("   every unordered triangle product is unchanged")


def demonstrate_edge_deletion_update() -> None:
    """Verify Δ tr(S^3) = 12(S^2)_ab for deletion of an existing edge."""
    n = 7
    edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 4), (1, 5),
             (2, 3), (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 6)}
    edge = (0, 1)
    s = seidel_matrix(n, edges)
    s2 = matmul(s, s)
    old_cube = spectral_moments(s)[2]
    reduced = seidel_matrix(n, delete_edge(edges, edge))
    new_cube = spectral_moments(reduced)[2]
    predicted = 12 * s2[edge[0]][edge[1]]
    observed = new_cube - old_cube
    assert observed == predicted
    print("\n3. Local cubic update under edge deletion")
    print(f"   deleted edge={edge}, (S^2)_ab={s2[edge[0]][edge[1]]}")
    print(f"   old trace={old_cube}, new trace={new_cube}")
    print(f"   observed change={observed}, predicted change={predicted}")


def main() -> None:
    demonstrate_triangle_identity()
    demonstrate_switching()
    demonstrate_edge_deletion_update()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Numerical demonstrations of Seidel moments and triangle holonomy.

The script uses only the Python standard library.  It constructs Seidel matrices,
computes exact traces by integer matrix arithmetic, enumerates triple parities,
checks switching invariance, and verifies the local cubic update after deleting
an edge.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Iterable, Sequence

Matrix = list[list[int]]
Edge = tuple[int, int]


def normalize_edges(edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> set[Edge]:
    """Return undirected edges as sorted endpoint pairs."""
    return {tuple(sorted((a, b))) for a, b in edges if a != b}


def seidel_matrix(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> Matrix:
    """Construct the n-by-n Seidel matrix of a finite simple graph."""
    edge_set = normalize_edges(edges)
    return [
        [0 if i == j else (-1 if tuple(sorted((i, j))) in edge_set else 1)
         for j in range(n)]
        for i in range(n)
    ]


def matmul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Multiply two square integer matrices."""
    n = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(n))
             for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def trace(a: Matrix) -> int:
    """Return the trace of a square matrix."""
    return sum(a[i][i] for i in range(len(a)))


def spectral_moments(s: Matrix) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Return the first three exact moments tr(S), tr(S^2), tr(S^3)."""
    s2 = matmul(s, s)
    s3 = matmul(s2, s)
    return trace(s), trace(s2), trace(s3)


def triangle_parity_counts(n: int, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Count unordered vertex triples with even and odd induced edge counts."""
    edge_set = normalize_edges(edges)
    even = odd = 0
    for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
        count = sum(
            tuple(sorted(pair)) in edge_set
            for pair in ((i, j), (j, k), (k, i))
        )
        if count % 2 == 0:
            even += 1
        else:
            odd += 1
    return even, odd


def switch_matrix(s: Matrix, signs: Sequence[int]) -> Matrix:
    """Apply diagonal sign switching S_ij -> d_i S_ij d_j."""
    if len(s) != len(signs) or any(d not in (-1, 1) for d in signs):
        raise ValueError("signs must contain one value in {-1,+1} per vertex")
    return [[signs[i] * s[i][j] * signs[j] for j in range(len(s))]
            for i in range(len(s))]


def delete_edge(edges: Iterable[Edge], edge: Edge) -> set[Edge]:
    """Delete one undirected edge from an edge set."""
    result = normalize_edges(edges)
    target = tuple(sorted(edge))
    if target not in result:
        raise ValueError(f"{target} is not an edge")
    result.remove(target)
    return result


def demonstrate_triangle_identity() -> None:
    """Compare cubic matrix traces with six times the parity imbalance."""
    examples = {
        "empty triangle": (3, set()),
        "complete triangle": (3, {(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)}),
        "five-cycle": (5, {(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0)}),
    }
    print("1. Cubic trace as signed triple parity")
    for name, (n, edges) in examples.items():
        moments = spectral_moments(seidel_matrix(n, edges))
        even, odd = triangle_parity_counts(n, edges)
        parity_value = 6 * (even - odd)
        assert moments[2] == parity_value
        assert moments[0] == 0 and moments[1] == n * (n - 1)
        print(f"   {name:18s}: moments={moments}, "
              f"(N_even,N_odd)=({even},{odd}), 6Δ={parity_value}")


def demonstrate_switching() -> None:
    """Show that triangle holonomy and the cubic trace survive switching."""
    n = 6
    edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 5)}
    signs = (-1, 1, -1, 1, 1, -1)
    s = seidel_matrix(n, edges)
    switched = switch_matrix(s, signs)
    before = spectral_moments(s)
    after = spectral_moments(switched)
    for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
        lhs = switched[i][j] * switched[j][k] * switched[k][i]
        rhs = s[i][j] * s[j][k] * s[k][i]
        assert lhs == rhs
    assert before == after
    print("\n2. Switching invariance")
    print(f"   signs={signs}")
    print(f"   moments before={before}, after={after}")
    print("   every unordered triangle product is unchanged")

    """Verify Δ tr(S^3) = 12(S^2)_ab for deletion of an existing edge."""
    n = 7
    edges = {(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 4), (1, 5),
             (2, 3), (2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 6)}
    edge = (0, 1)
    s = seidel_matrix(n, edges)
    s2 = matmul(s, s)
    old_cube = spectral_moments(s)[2]
    reduced = seidel_matrix(n, delete_edge(edges, edge))
    new_cube = spectral_moments(reduced)[2]
    predicted = 12 * s2[edge[0]][edge[1]]
    observed = new_cube - old_cube

    print("\n3. Local cubic update under edge deletion")
    print(f"   deleted edge={edge}, (S^2)_ab={s2[edge[0]][edge[1]]}")
    print(f"   old trace={old_cube}, new trace={new_cube}")
    print(f"   observed change={observed}, predicted change={predicted}")


def main() -> None:
    demonstrate_triangle_identity()
    demonstrate_switching()
    demonstrate_edge_deletion_update()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import Mathlib

/-!
# What random proof-step opening does—and does not—guarantee

This file gives a finite, information-theoretic analysis of the protocol proposed in
the prompt.  A verifier asks for a coordinate of a witness and receives that coordinate
in the clear.  We characterize perfect zero knowledge for this protocol, show a concrete
privacy failure, and quantify why checking one uniformly random proof line does not by
itself give soundness error `2⁻ᵏ`.

No computational hardness assumption is modeled.  Consequently the results concern
perfect (not computational) zero knowledge.
-/

namespace ZeroKnowledge

/-- Perfect witness-independence of a deterministic verifier view. -/
def PerfectWitnessPrivacy {S W V : Type*} (valid : S → W → Prop)
    (view : S → W → V) : Prop :=
  ∀ s w₁ w₂, valid s w₁ → valid s w₂ → view s w₁ = view s w₂

/-- The view produced by opening coordinate `i` of a finite witness. -/
def openingView {S A : Type*} (i : Fin n) (_statement : S)
    (witness : Fin n → A) : A := witness i

/-
Opening a coordinate is perfectly witness-private exactly when every two valid
witnesses agree at that coordinate.
-/
theorem openingView_private_iff {S A : Type*} (valid : S → (Fin n → A) → Prop)
    (i : Fin n) :
    PerfectWitnessPrivacy valid (openingView i) ↔
      ∀ s w₁ w₂, valid s w₁ → valid s w₂ → w₁ i = w₂ i := by
  constructor <;> intro h <;> exact h

/-
If two valid witnesses differ in the challenged coordinate, revealing that
coordinate is not perfect zero knowledge.
-/
theorem openingView_not_private {S A : Type*} (valid : S → (Fin n → A) → Prop)
    (i : Fin n) (s : S) (w₁ w₂ : Fin n → A)
    (h₁ : valid s w₁) (h₂ : valid s w₂) (hne : w₁ i ≠ w₂ i) :
    ¬ PerfectWitnessPrivacy valid (openingView i) := by
  exact fun h => hne ( h s w₁ w₂ h₁ h₂ )

/-
Revealing *every possible* coordinate is private only when the valid witness is
unique extensionally.  Randomizing which coordinate is revealed does not remove this
obstruction, since the challenge itself is part of the transcript.
-/
theorem all_openings_private_iff_unique {S A : Type*}
    (valid : S → (Fin n → A) → Prop) :
    (∀ i, PerfectWitnessPrivacy valid (openingView i)) ↔
      ∀ s w₁ w₂, valid s w₁ → valid s w₂ → w₁ = w₂ := by
  -- Fix an $i$.
  apply Iff.intro;
  · intro h s w₁ w₂ hw₁ hw₂; ext i; exact h i s w₁ w₂ hw₁ hw₂;
  · intro h i s w₁ w₂ h₁ h₂ ; have := h s w₁ w₂ h₁ h₂ ; aesop;

/-- A concrete two-witness relation for which opening coordinate zero leaks the secret. -/
def bitWitnessValid (_statement : Unit) (_witness : Fin 1 → Bool) : Prop := True

/-
The naive opening protocol fails perfect witness privacy even for a one-bit witness.
-/
theorem bit_opening_leaks :
    ¬ PerfectWitnessPrivacy bitWitnessValid (openingView (0 : Fin 1)) := by
  -- By definition of `openingView`, we have that `openingView 0 (fun _ => false) ≠ openingView 0 (fun _ => true)`.
  simp [PerfectWitnessPrivacy, bitWitnessValid, openingView] at *;
  exists fun _ => Bool.true, fun _ => Bool.false

/-- Exact false-acceptance probability after `k` independent repetitions when one out
of `n` equally likely checks catches the error.  The definition is meaningful for
`n > 0`; callers carry that condition. -/
def singleBadFailure (n k : ℕ) : ℚ := (((n - 1 : ℕ) : ℚ) / n) ^ k

/-
With four possible checks and only one bad location, `k` repetitions have failure
probability `(3/4)^k`, not `(1/2)^k`.
-/
theorem four_check_failure (k : ℕ) :
    singleBadFailure 4 k = (3 / 4 : ℚ) ^ k := by
  unfold singleBadFailure; norm_num;

strictly greater than the advertised `2⁻ᵏ` bound.
-/
theorem four_check_not_binary_sound (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) :

soundness bound: choosing `n = 2k+2` leaves more than half the probability mass on
challenge sequences which miss a single bad location.
